name: Wrestling Up from Guard
keyCorrections: If they sprawl on the wrestle-up: drop back to guard and try a different entry (shin-to-shin or 2-on-1)
If they guillotine you: your head was too tall — keep your forehead to their chest or jaw as you stand
If you cannot find the leg: they posted back — switch to the front headlock using your underhook grip
description: Wrestle up from seated or butterfly guard using shin-to-shin, 2-on-1, or underhook to convert to a single leg or front headlock. Wrestling up is the primary offensive transition from guard — it converts bottom position into a takedown opportunity.
shortInstruction: From seated guard, win the underhook or 2-on-1, create a hip angle, post your outside foot, and drive to a single leg. If the single leg is blocked, transition to a front headlock or back take.
summary: Wrestling up from guard transforms guard from a defensive position into an offensive takedown entry. The sequence uses either an underhook, shin-to-shin, or 2-on-1 to control the opponent's upper body while you stand. From standing, you finish with a single leg, body lock, or front headlock. Wrestling up is the core of the modern no-gi guard system — every seated guard player must have a reliable wrestle-up to prevent the opponent from standing and passing.
whyItWorks: Wrestling up punishes the opponent for standing in your guard — if they stand, you come up with them
The underhook and 2-on-1 give you upper body control that prevents them from sprawling or crossfacing
Shin-to-shin entry prevents the opponent from stepping back when you stand — your shin blocks their leg
The wrestle-up creates a dilemma for the passer: they must either engage (and risk the sweep) or disengage (and give up the pass attempt)
commonMistakes: Trying to wrestle up without upper body control — they will sprawl and flatten you
Standing straight instead of staying low — a tall stand exposes the single leg and guillotine
Not creating a hip angle before standing — standing straight at them gives them an easy sprawl angle
Giving up on the wrestle-up too early — commit to the stand or you will be stuck in a compromised position
coachingCues: Stay low, drive to the leg
safetySummary: Do not stand with a straight back — this exposes the guillotine and gives up the underhook
If the opponent sprawls as you stand, drop back to guard rather than fighting the sprawl
Be careful of knee strain when posting from seated guard — warm up properly

systemLogic.corePrinciple: The wrestle-up from guard has three entry systems: Underhook Entry → Shin-to-Shin Entry → 2-on-1 Entry

decisionTree.action: from seated guard, pummel for an underhook on one side. Your other hand posts on the mat. As you stand, the underhook prevents them from sprawling. Finish with a single leg or body lock
enter shin-to-shin guard by placing your shin across their near shin. As you stand, the shin blocks their leg from stepping back. Come up to a single leg on the same side

secure both hands on one of their arms (wrist and elbow). Pull the arm across your body as you stand. The 2-on-1 neutralizes their ability to post or sprawl. Finish by circling behind or attacking the single leg
each entry leads to the same finishes: single leg, body lock, front headlock, or back take

moneyDetails: Wrestling up is the most important offensive skill in modern no-gi guard — without it, your guard is purely defensive
Mastering the wrestle-up gives you the ability to score takedowns from guard, transforming your entire bottom game
Wrestling up is a core component of all high-level no-gi guard systems (Dewey, Meregali, Ruotolos)
fixItFast: If they stand and disengage: stand up fully and re-engage from neutral — do not stay seated
If they pressure forward: use their momentum — wrestle-up into their forward drive
If they circle to pass: circle with them and maintain the underhook or 2-on-1
